Modern Quick Dev: Learning and Building the Hard Way
A hands-on journey through building the Geekroom reveal website with React, React Bits, Vite, and Vercel. Learning the workflow while making mistakes along the way.
A hands-on journey through building the Geekroom reveal website with React, React Bits, Vite, and Vercel—learning the workflow while making mistakes along the way.

![Geekroom reveal website banner](geekroom-banner.png) > **Disclaimer:** Due to my Windows installation getting corrupted after an update, my original files have been lost. My GitHub only has the production package, not the development build, so the website may not function correctly if you check it. (2nd August 2026) ## The Beginning Making any website requires an understanding of both function and design to allow users to understand, use, and connect with it and its purpose. This will be more of a journey about how to—and how not to—create a website: the reason behind certain decisions, the story behind the final result, the mistakes, and the things learnt along the way. ### “Quick Dev” and “Hard Way”? Before starting this, my experience with web development only extended to HTML and CSS, with some brief work in JS and PHP on one of my previous projects. When it came to making this website, it needed to be simple yet impactful. With a short timeline, I couldn't just sit down, allocate time to learning React, and then make the site. I had to learn it on the fly as I was making the site. That’s why “Quick Dev” refers to quickly learning the basic developer workflow for a framework. “Hard Way,” on the other hand, refers to the mistakes I made along the way. There were a lot, mostly rooted in oversight, which resulted in reworking and fixing things. But if there’s one thing I learnt along the way, it is: > “It's better to check the best method than to believe you can handle it later.” You will soon find out why. ## The Basics ### React ![React logo](react-logo.jpg) React is a free and open-source front-end JavaScript library that aims to make building user interfaces based on components more seamless. It is maintained by Meta and a community of individual developers and companies. — From Wikipedia React basically allows you to use what they call “components” directly in your project, which usually resides in `App.jsx`. What JSX is, and the file structure of React applications, will be touched on later. For now, we need to understand the basics. Ideally, when you use basic HTML, CSS, and JS, you keep the structure in HTML, the style in CSS, and the functioning in JS. Here it's a little different. You have an `App.jsx` where you make your web page and call components to be used. Your `App.jsx` has its own `index.css`, and the components exist as their own `.jsx` files and may or may not have their own `.css` files. This allows developers to use components created by other developers with ease, allowing you to focus more on creating the web page rather than creating the components from scratch. Let's take a small example. The article demonstrates importing a `LightRays` component from `@/components/LightRays`, placing it inside the app's returned JSX, and configuring its properties (such as the ray origin, colour, speed, length, and mouse-follow behaviour). ![Light rays component example](light-rays-demo.jpg) As you can see, the `App.jsx` calls a component named `LightRays` that exists in the `/components/LightRays` folder. We then make a `div` in the return for the `App()` function and use the `LightRays` component in the same manner as an HTML element, with its modifiable values. This is what makes React a great way to implement beautiful, functional components with ease onto our web page. As for where I got the component, that's where React Bits comes into the picture. ### React Bits ![React Bits website](react-bits-homepage.jpg) React Bits allows you to use modern, highly customisable components with easy implementation. It is 100% free and open source, allowing you to make edits to the components with ease. Nearly all of the components I used for this project came from here, and I can say it is a component library I had a ton of fun using. It consists of everything from text effects, animations, and navigation components to backgrounds and much more. The components can be installed via the command line or manually, and all the steps are available on the pages for each component. There's one more thing: hosting the website online. ### Vercel ![Vercel website](vercel-homepage.jpg) To deploy the site online, I used Vercel. It allows users to deploy sites by giving Vercel access to the GitHub repository that contains the build of your webpage. More on deployment later. ## The Beginning I will try finishing the website as soon as possible. *September 17, 2025* For some context, we needed to make the students of our college aware of the upcoming orientation event of our club. For it, we needed a site, and I, as the Vice-President, decided to take the initiative so that I could learn and create a site that I could deploy online via Vercel. As for why a site and not a simple brochure: it has become a standard that every club must have a website. Because of this, I concluded that a website is a necessary requirement for our club, which can be extended in the future. So here was the game plan: - Make the webpage using React. - Publish it using Vercel. So yeah, let's see how to do that. ## The Prerequisites ### A Code Editor ![Visual Studio Code website](vscode-homepage.jpg) You can use any code editor of your choice. I used Visual Studio Code, however, you can definitely use other tools like Notepad++ (I also see you Vim users—dare I say I love it too). ### Node.js ![Node.js website](nodejs-homepage.jpg) I used Node.js in my project. It comes with npm, a package manager that allows us to manage libraries and modules, which will also allow us to install and use the React library. It also comes with Vite, a compiler and bundler that allows us to create development servers and create builds of our website that are lightweight and can be used across the web. ## The Process First thing I had to do was install Node.js. One heads-up I would like to give is that you should note down the location where you are installing it, because you will have to add that directory to PATH on Windows. This process will be different on other operating systems, but the idea is the same. ![Windows environment variables](windows-environment-variables.jpg) Okay, let's see how we can create a React application. First make a folder on your PC for the website to live in, then on the command line in the same directory, use either of the following commands: ```bash npm create vite@latest ``` or ```bash npm create vite@latest ``` The `` just allows you to quickly mention your application folder name; otherwise, it will ask anyway. The command launches the Vite project setup. It will guide you to select the framework we need: React. ![Vite and React starter screen](vite-react-starter.jpg) For the variant, we will select TypeScript, as React Bits requires it. The setup also asks whether to use `rolldown-vite` (experimental). It is not needed here. You can choose to install with npm and start now, which lets you immediately run a development server. The terminal should show Vite running, with a local address such as `http://localhost:5173`. If you follow the localhost link, it will show the default Vite + React webpage. Yay! Our webpage with Vite and React! Just to make sure everything is there, make sure you are in the folder of your created website and run: ```bash npm i ``` or ```bash npm install ``` This will install any necessary packages that may not have been installed. ## The Project Structure Let's clear the things that you should and shouldn't do. Let's see the file structure right now. ![Initial project file structure](project-structure-initial.jpg) There's a lot to unpack here, so let's just highlight the main files we would be working with. ![Main files in the project](main-files-structure.jpg) These are the main files we will be working with, whereas the other files are a one-time setup. ![One-time setup files](setup-files-structure.jpg) Our goal is to have a directory structure like the one below: ![Target project directory structure](target-project-structure.jpg) As we can see, it's a clean directory structure with components existing in their own folder, and the main page separated (the `pages` folder exists as this is a multi-page site). Our objective is to avoid the mistakes below: ![Incorrect project directory structure](incorrect-project-structure.jpg) See the problem? No `components` folder, `tsconfig.json` missing, and most importantly, one `.css` file with the CSS of all the components and the main page existing together. Let's see how to avoid these mistakes by seeing how we can use React Bits components in our project while avoiding common mistakes. ## Using Components Just to be clear, there are many component libraries online, but we will constrain ourselves to React Bits. Let's say we want to use a React Bits background like the one below. ### Liquid Ether ![Liquid Ether component preview](liquid-ether-demo.jpg) It's a background that reacts to the user's mouse movement and, when not affected, runs a default loop. For my use case, we will first make sure that at the top right of the page we select **JS** and **CSS**. ![Select JavaScript and CSS](react-bits-language-selector.jpg) This is because I made the site with React Bits components that use basic `.js` and CSS. Hey! Why did we select TypeScript earlier? We used TypeScript because certain components require it. For example, if I remove my `tsconfig.json` file and try installing any component, we will be hit with this: > No import alias found in your tsconfig.json file. Visit the shadcn installation documentation to learn how to set an import alias. So make sure to have these files, because while we will be using simple JS and CSS components, we would still need these files. Now let's see how to use these components. 1. Select **Code**. 2. Copy the code. 3. Select **Install**, and make sure you have selected **CLI** and **npm**. 4. Copy the command and run it in the command line. ![React Bits code selection](react-bits-code-tab.jpg) The installation panel provides a CLI command for the selected component: ![React Bits install command](react-bits-install-command.jpg) The CLI may ask whether you need to create a `components.json` file to add components. Proceed with **yes**. ![Component installation command](component-install-command.jpg) ### Fixing the Tailwind CSS and import-alias issues The installation may report that no Tailwind CSS configuration was found and that no import alias was found in `tsconfig.json`. On the first line, we said yes because we do need a separate `components.json` for managing component versions. The next block of text says that we don't have Tailwind CSS installed. The last one states that we don't have an import alias in our `tsconfig.json` file. Let's fix all this, starting with the first block. #### Tailwind CSS ![Tailwind CSS website](tailwindcss-homepage.jpg) Tailwind CSS is a CSS library that allows you to style elements more quickly by implementing classes directly in your HTML element. For example, instead of creating a separate CSS class and styling it in a CSS file: ```html The Span ``` you can write the styling directly in the class: ```html The new Span ``` As we can see, the new span now has its styling content in it, and we don't require a separate CSS rule for it, as Tailwind CSS will apply it directly based on what is written in the class. If you wish, you can use Tailwind in your project. However, we need it because the background elements of React Bits use Tailwind. To add Tailwind CSS, the article gives this command: ```bash npm install tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite ``` After it is done, we will go to `vite.config.js` and add the Tailwind Vite plugin: ```js import { defineConfig } from 'vite' import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react' import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite' export default defineConfig({ plugins: [react(), tailwindcss()], }) ``` ![Tailwind CSS configuration in Vite and index.css](tailwind-install-config-code.jpg) And add this to the top of the `index.css` file: ```css @import "tailwindcss"; ``` #### Fixing the import alias Now we will solve the second part of this. To fix the import alias, we will go into our `tsconfig.json`. In it, we will see the project references to: ```json { "files": [], "references": [ { "path": "./tsconfig.app.json" }, { "path": "./tsconfig.node.json" } ] } ``` To this, we will add `compilerOptions` with a base URL and path alias. The example shown in the article is: ```json { "files": [], "references": [ { "path": "./tsconfig.app.json" }, { "path": "./tsconfig.node.json" } ], "compilerOptions": { "baseUrl": ".", "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } } } ``` And that's it. Now when we copy the component's install command and run it, it will create a `components` folder in which the components will be added. ## Using the Component To use the component in your project, just go to **Usage**. ![Liquid Ether usage code](liquid-ether-usage-code.jpg) The article also shows an example of keeping component imports together at the top of the app file: ![Example component imports](react-bits-import-example.jpg) Copy the above and paste it in your file. It is advised to have all your imports at the very top of your `App.jsx`. From here, you may now explore ways to make your website as interactive and beautiful as you wish, and learn how divisions work on these components. To see your project in localhost, run: ```bash npm run dev ``` ## The Final Leg Now that you have a website, you will need the world to see it. For that, we will use Vercel. ![Vercel deployment page](vercel-deployment.jpg) To host on Vercel, we will need it on a public GitHub repository and a Vercel account, so make one. Then on your terminal run: ```bash npm run build ``` This will make a `dist` folder in which your final build will be made for production. This is the folder you are going to put in your GitHub repository. ### Optional Step If you want speed insights and an analytics dashboard to work on Vercel for your site, do the following. In your terminal, run: ```bash npm install @vercel/analytics npm install @vercel/speed-insights ``` And in your `App.jsx`, just add: ```jsx import { SpeedInsights } from "@vercel/speed-insights/react"; import { Analytics } from "@vercel/analytics/react"; ``` These can be added anywhere in the component's returned JSX. In your GitHub repository, just add your `dist` folder, go on Vercel, and follow its guide to add the GitHub repository. Voilà! You will have it up and running. ## The Destination: The Website ![Geekroom final website](geekroom-final-website.jpg) I started with the idea of finishing it in one day; it took me 20 days. It wasn't easy, but it was a great learning experience, and there is still a lot to learn, like Google indexing, which… I'll just say I'm getting there, and you will know once it's done. Still, just using beautiful components isn't enough to make a website. Planning and research are key in order to create a website. ### What's next? Well, as of writing this, I have indexed it on Google, meaning my website can be searched for. However, there are more things to be done to make the indexing better, so I am planning on learning more about Google search indexing. ### What We Learned 1. Using React and components. 2. Learned hosting using Vercel. 3. Using components from React Bits. 4. Making correct file structures. ---
Documenting my journey from scanning a real hand with photogrammetry to 3D printing it, including the cleanup, slicing, and printer problems along the way.

![wow](SplitScreen.png)

*Photogrammetry* and *3D printing* are an *art form*, an art of knowing the best methods to capture images for photogrammetry and knowing the right temperature, print speed and modeling decisions for the parts to be printed.

Most of the "art" in 3D printing is attributed to the 3D printer itself, as different printer models require different levels of "involvement" during the printing process.

Let me set the scene for what I have and what objectives I am fulfilling.

# The Printer

![Creality Ender V3 Pro](Printer.png)


The printer at my disposal is a Creality Ender V3 Pro, it is cheap & reliable, just not consistent. We'll talk about it in a bit.

I have access to this printer through the incubation center in my college.

# The Filament
![Green PLA filament](Filament.png)
Most prints you will see below are done using PLA. It is biodegradable and is the most commonly used filament in 3D printing.


# The project

I have been assigned the task of 3D printing a hand, 3D scanned by me.
The first step is obviously 3D scanning the hand.

**The 3D scanned hand after processing**
![The 3D scanned hand after processing](FinalHand.png)



The method of 3D scanning I used to achieve the result is using **Photogrammetry**. It is the practice of creating 3D models by *capturing the pictures of the subject in an ordered, orbital fashion* i.e. capturing images by circling around the subject in small steps and taking multiple pictures of said subject.

**Example from Wikipedia**
![Photogrammetry example from Wikipedia](ExampleWiki.png)



As we can see in the above image, the following was generated using photos taken by circling around the building. Similarly, we can generate 3D models for any subject.

To process the images, you need dedicated software.

# The Software
**Meshroom**
![Meshroom](Meshroom.png)

One free application is **Meshroom**, it is free and open-source and can be used to process images for 3D model creation. It is however resource intensive and expects you to have a decently powerful PC.

If you have an internet connection and some programming knowledge, you can definitely use this [*notebook*](#) to make these models, most of the models of my subjects are made using this Colab notebook.

However, for this hand, I used a different application.

**Polycam**
![Polycam](Polycam.png)



**Polycam** is available on the Apple App Store and is a suite of photogrammetry solutions, wrapped in a single app, that can be used to make 3D models and even Gaussian splats.

It was an easy process, just orbit around the subject and capture pictures.

or so it seemed...

---

# Model Cleaning
**Raw models (left), Final model (right, highlighted)**
![Raw models (left), final model (right, highlighted)](RawModels.png)

We took 2 scans of the entire arm, one gave a good raw of the arm, the other gave a good raw of the hand.

The scan was expected to be done with the intent to have both the hand and the arm in a single model.

However, in one scan, the subject closed his hand due to fatigue, in the other one, the application only returned the hand.

**Converting raw to final**
![Converting raw to final](RawToFinal.png)



The solution was to **remove the unwanted areas**, attach the hand onto the arm and then process the model by smoothening and fixing the details through sculpting in Blender.

But first, the models needed their different parts connected together into a single closed polygon.

## Meshlab
**Meshlab**
![Meshlab](MeshlabImport.png)


We **import** the scanned models in **Meshlab** for processing. Our first intent is to **join the different edges into one**. What do I mean by joining the different edges? To answer that, first go here:

**On the right pane**

![On the right pane](MeshlabRightPane.png)



And turn Boundary edges on:

**Boundary Edges On**

![Boundary Edges On](BoundaryEdgesToggle.png)



You will see this:

![Boundary edges](BoundaryEdges.png)

We can see **lines** highlighted across the model. These lines are enclosed and are actually the boundary of different polygons *aligned* together to form the hand.

The reason I say aligned is because their coordinates and rotations place them into the positions they are in to represent a hand, however if I sculpt on it in Blender, it will not work as intended, so we need to join them together.

To do so:

1. Select **Merge Close Vertices**

![We will select Merge Close Vertices](MergeCloseVerticesMenu.png)


2. Click **Apply**

![Merge Close Vertices dialog](MergeCloseVerticesDialog.png)


**Voila**

![The merged result](MergedResult.png)



As we can see, the moment we click apply, the model will show **no boundary edges**. This is the intended output.

Now we will export it as .obj:

![Export Mesh As](MeshlabFileMenu.png)

![Choosing the .obj file type](MeshlabExportObj.png)

The same was done by me on the other mesh.

## Blender

In Blender the .obj can be imported from the files as usual, no need to import the .mtl files, 3D printing does not require textures.

**Importing .obj**
![Importing .obj](BlenderImportObj.png)



Now we intend on removing the red parts of our model.

**Area to delete**
![Area to delete](AreaToDelete.png)



I do so by going into edit mode with wireframe mode on, selecting the areas and deleting them in both the models:

**Deleting faces**
![Deleting faces](DeletingFaces.png)



Not going into too much detail as I don't have a save file for every step, but basically after I removed the unnecessary polygons I did the following:

1. **Place both models at the desired location:**

![Both models placed](PlaceModels.png)

2. **Use shrinkwrap to connect both sections**

Okay so basically, instead of retopology, I went for using the shrinkwrap modifier to make a *glove in a sense*, to wrap the entire hand and then use that as the main model.

![Shrink wrap](ShrinkWrap.png)

*Shrink wrap*

Above is an example image, I have used a simple cube with a subdivision modifier applied first and then the shrinkwrap applied:

![Subdivision and shrinkwrap modifiers](ShrinkWrapModifiers.png)

In practice, I had made a model using a **subdivided cube** whose modifier was not applied and made a simplified model covering the entire hand and then shrinkwrapped it:

![A cube being edited while the subdivision modifier is still active](SubdivisionCube.png)

*A cube being edited while subdivision modifier is still active*

3. **Sculpt details and clean the model**

The rest of it was done using the sculpting tools in Blender to fix the model and get it ready for 3D printing.

![Before (left) and after (right)](BeforeAfter.png)

*Before (left), after (right)*

4. **Export as .obj**

![Exporting as .obj](BlenderExportObj.png)

*Exporting as .obj*

---

# 3D Printing

Now back to 3D printing. First we need to choose settings for the print and the placement of the model being printed on the print tray. For this there are 2 different software options you can use.

1. **Ultimaker Cura**

![Ultimaker Cura](UltimakerCura.png)

*Ultimaker Cura*

**Ultimaker Cura** is an open-source slicing software for 3D printing, I use this when I need to make simple prints, however for this project, I used another tool.

2. **Bamboo Studio**

![Bamboo Studio](BambooStudio.png)

**Bamboo Studio** is another open-source tool for slicing and the one I used for this project. Let's address the challenges of the print.

# Challenges

1. **Print Size**

![Printer size (left), print size (right)](PrinterSize.png)

*Printer size (left), Print Size (right)*

The main problem is that our hand model is 420 mm in the Z axis (height). We need to **cut** the model into 2 parts in order to print the complete model in the same space.

2. **Print time and material used**

We need to make sure that the material used is not more than what is needed and the print time is manageable.

## Tackling the challenges

First let's import the model.

![Imported model](BambooStudio.png)

*Imported model*

As we can see, it is quite small. Fortunately, I know that the model is 420 mm in height, so I will change the model Z-axis height to 420 mm.

![Z-axis height changed to 420mm](ScaleZ.png)

*Z-axis height changed to 420mm*

Make sure **uniform scale** is **toggled**.

Now we face our first challenge, the **print exceeds the print size** due to its **height**.

![Error message](HeightError.png)

*Error message*

To fix this we will use the **cut tool**.

![Cut tool](CutTool.png)

*Cut tool*

Once it is at the desired location, we will go to **add connectors**.

![Connectors](Connectors.png)

Select **square connector**, as it reduces the chances of the connection rotating compared to a circular connection, while still being a strong connection with **minimal filament usage**.

Change whatever parameters you need to, click on the location you want it at, and click confirm, then on the cut menu, click confirm.

![Cut result](CutResult1.png)

*Result*

![Cut result, close-up of the connector](CutResult2.png)

*Result*

This is the result of the cut, now we place the models in the desired locations on the tray.

![Laid within the print area](LaidOnPlate.png)

*Laid within the print area*

Now let's see what happens if we slice it as is with the default settings.

![Slice plate](SlicePlateButton.png)

![Slicing result with default settings](SliceDefault.png)

Okay, that's a lot of print time and material being used. Let's fix this.

First of all, this print is for **showcase** and poses **no functional purpose** other than **viewing**, so it needs to be strong enough to survive minor hits, but has no need to be extremely strong; for this, we will change the *infill amount*.

## Infill

![Sparse infill settings](InfillSettings.png)

*Sparse Infill (bottom)*

In the strength tab at the bottom we have **infill density**.

![Grid infill](GridInfill.png)

*Grid infill*

**Infill** is used to **increase part strength** by filling the interior hull with an infill pattern, the *higher the infill percent, the stronger the material.* As it's for showcase, I will decrease it to 1%.

![Reduced to 1%](InfillOnePercent.png)

*Reduced to 1%*

I will also make sure that the wall loop is at least 3. Now if I check the print time:

![Print and material amount used](SliceReduced.png)

*Print and material amount used*

That is a substantial decrease, however, the incubation center is open from 9:30 AM to 5 PM, so I need to decrease it even more. Fortunately for us, I can select which part is printable:

![Printable option in the right-click menu](PrintableMenu.png)

*After right clicking with a part selected*

![Part selected as not printable, hidden](PartHidden.png)

*Part selected as not printable (hidden)*

Now let's see the time for just printing the hand:

![Slicing result for the hand only](SliceHandOnly.png)

*Print time*

It's 7 hrs, just within the time I am provided. The other one takes 12 hrs, but I can take permission to print that so no worries.

Oh, also the other part needs **supports**, so you can easily turn those on here:

![Supports](Supports.png)

*Supports*

We can now export it as a G-code file to our printer:

![Export G-code file](ExportGcode.png)

*Export button*

# Preparing the printer

To prepare the printer we first need to **calibrate** it, i.e. dial in the print speed, temperature and other details.

Most people use the calibration cube:

![Calibration cube](CalibrationCube.png)

*Calibration Cube*

I like to use:

![Print in Place Ragdollbot on Printables](Ragdollbot.png)

*Ragdollbot*

Because it takes just an hour and yeah... it's kinda cool.

Now during the calibration test, I fortunately faced only 2 problems with simple fixes:

1. **Filament got stuck in the nozzle**

![Improper flow](ImproperFlow1.png)

*Improper flow*

![Improper flow](ImproperFlow2.png)

*Improper flow*

The **flow** of the filament became **inconsistent**, it was because the tray was too high and it resulted in the nozzle rubbing into the print and making the filament clog the nozzle partially or completely.

The fix was easy:

![Tray height adjuster](TrayHeight.png)

*Tray height adjuster*

I had to adjust the tray height, purge a small amount of the filament and continue.

2. **Filament jamming**

![Later layers didn't print](FilamentJamming.png)

*Later layers didn't print*

![Later layers didn't print, close-up](LaterLayers.png)

*Later layers didn't print*

This was because of the printer filament getting stuck in the spool:

![Filament crossing](FilamentCrossing.png)

*Filament crossing*

To fix this I corrected the crossing over of the filament in the spool.

This is a **temporary** fix. The filament pulling mechanism is strong enough to fix the spool itself, however the spool is placed at the center of the top bar:

![Spool placement](SpoolPlacement.png)

*Spool placement*

This gives the pulling mechanism a sharp angle resulting in lowered pulling force and more friction on the filament itself:

![Jamming filament](JammingFilament.png)

*Jamming filament*

A more **permanent** solution is given by this [Reddit user](#), but for it I will need some spare parts:

![Reddit solution](RedditSolution.png)

*Reddit*

But for now, manual correction does the job.

# Output

![Partial print of the hand (in focus) and ragdoll (out of focus)](PartialPrint.png)

*Partial print of the hand (in focus) and ragdoll (out of focus)*

Here is the partial print of the hand and the calibration ragdoll. The ragdoll has been printed *beautifully* and the interior of the hand has thick walls with a *good slot shape and infill wall.*

# What I learned

I have improved my sculpting skills in Blender and also learnt how to use Bamboo Studio and Meshlab.

I have also learnt how to do better captures for photogrammetry and best practices for 3D printing and model cleaning.
